21.why_open: Allows file transfers between client and server over a network
21.who_uses: Web developers uploading files, legacy systems performing automated transfers
21.who_exploits: Attackers performing anonymous login attempts, credential sniffing, and bounce attacks
21.risk: Credentials and file contents transmitted in plaintext — full interception possible
how_to_fix: Disable FTP entirely and replace with SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol)
If FTP is required, enforce FTPS (FTP over TLS) for encrypted transport
Disable anonymous FTP login in the server configuration
Restrict FTP access to specific IP addresses via firewall rules
Audit all files accessible via FTP and remove sensitive data
21.real_world_example: CVE-2011-2523 — vsftpd 2.3.4 backdoor allowing remote command execution on port 6200

22.why_open: Provides encrypted remote access to the server for administrative tasks
22.who_uses: System administrators, developers, and DevOps engineers for remote login
22.who_exploits: Attackers using brute-force tools, credential stuffing, or stolen private keys
22.risk: Full remote compromise of the system — attacker gains complete shell access
how_to_fix: Disable root login: set PermitRootLogin no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config
Disable password authentication — enforce SSH key-based login only
Change the default port from 22 to a non-standard port above 1024
Install and configure fail2ban to block brute-force attempts automatically
Restrict SSH access to specific IP addresses using firewall rules
22.real_world_example: CVE-2018-15473 — OpenSSH 7.7 username enumeration vulnerability exploited in targeted attacks

23.why_open: Legacy remote administration protocol — predates SSH
23.who_uses: Legacy network devices, embedded systems, and outdated server configurations
23.who_exploits: Attackers performing man-in-the-middle attacks and credential sniffing on the network
23.risk: All data including usernames and passwords transmitted in cleartext — trivially interceptable
how_to_fix: Disable Telnet immediately — there is no valid justification for its use in 2024
Replace with SSH for all remote administration requirements
Block port 23 on all network firewalls without exception
Audit all devices still running Telnet and schedule immediate replacement
23.real_world_example: CVE-2020-10188 — Telnet server vulnerability in multiple network device firmware allowing remote code execution

25.why_open: Mail server accepting or relaying outbound email messages
25.who_uses: Mail servers, web applications sending transactional email, internal mail relays
25.who_exploits: Spammers using open relays, attackers probing for mail server misconfigurations
25.risk: Open relay exploitation allowing the server to send spam globally — potential blacklisting and reputational damage
how_to_fix: Disable open relay — restrict SMTP to authenticated users only
Implement SPF, DKIM, and DMARC DNS records to prevent spoofing
Use port 587 (submission) with STARTTLS for authenticated outbound mail
Monitor SMTP logs for unusual sending volumes or patterns
Block port 25 inbound on servers that do not need to receive mail directly
25.real_world_example: CVE-2020-7247 — OpenSMTPD remote code execution vulnerability allowing arbitrary command execution as root

53.why_open: Resolves domain names to IP addresses for the network
53.who_uses: DNS servers, resolvers, and any system providing name resolution services
53.who_exploits: Attackers performing DNS amplification attacks, cache poisoning, and zone transfer abuse
53.risk: DNS amplification can be used in large-scale DDoS attacks; cache poisoning can redirect users to malicious sites
how_to_fix: Disable recursive queries for external/untrusted clients
Restrict zone transfers (AXFR) to authorized secondary servers only
Implement DNSSEC to prevent cache poisoning and spoofing
Rate-limit DNS responses to prevent amplification attack abuse
Keep DNS server software (BIND, PowerDNS) updated to the latest version
53.real_world_example: CVE-2020-1350 — SIGRed, a wormable Windows DNS Server remote code execution vulnerability

80.why_open: Web server serving unencrypted HTTP traffic on the standard web port
80.who_uses: Web browsers, web crawlers, API clients accessing web content
80.who_exploits: Attackers intercepting unencrypted traffic, performing injection attacks, and exploiting web application vulnerabilities
80.risk: All data transmitted in plaintext — session tokens, credentials, and content fully exposed to interception
how_to_fix: Redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS using a permanent 301 redirect
Obtain and install a valid TLS certificate (Let's Encrypt provides free certificates)
Enable HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) to prevent downgrade attacks
Disable HTTP entirely if all clients support HTTPS
Keep web server software (Apache, Nginx) updated to the latest stable version
80.real_world_example: CVE-2021-41773 — Apache HTTP Server 2.4.49 path traversal vulnerability enabling remote code execution

110.why_open: Mail retrieval protocol allowing email clients to download messages from a server
110.who_uses: Legacy email clients retrieving mail from a mailbox server
110.who_exploits: Attackers sniffing cleartext credentials transmitted during the authentication handshake
110.risk: Username and password are sent in plaintext unless wrapped in TLS — full credential exposure
how_to_fix: Disable plain POP3 and enforce POP3S (port 995) with TLS encryption
Require STARTTLS for all POP3 connections if port 110 must remain open
Migrate users to IMAP over TLS or modern protocols where possible
Monitor authentication logs for repeated failed login attempts
110.real_world_example: CVE-2020-12625 — Zimbra POP3 proxy vulnerability allowing credential exposure

139.service: NetBIOS — Network Basic Input Output System
139.why_open: Legacy Windows protocol providing name resolution and session services for file sharing
139.who_uses: Older Windows networks for file and printer sharing before SMB took over fully
139.who_exploits: Attackers performing NetBIOS enumeration to gather usernames, shares, and network information
139.risk: Information disclosure — attacker can enumerate shares, users, and system details to plan further attacks
how_to_fix: Disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP if not required for legacy compatibility
Block ports 137-139 at the network firewall from external access
Use modern SMB over port 445 with NetBIOS disabled where possible
Restrict NetBIOS access to trusted internal network segments only
139.real_world_example: CVE-2017-0144 — Related EternalBlue family vulnerability affecting NetBIOS/SMB stack on Windows

143.why_open: Mail retrieval protocol allowing clients to access and manage mailboxes on the server
143.who_uses: Email clients accessing mail while keeping messages synchronized on the server
143.who_exploits: Attackers intercepting cleartext credentials and session data when TLS is not enforced
143.risk: Credentials and email content exposed in plaintext — full mailbox compromise possible via interception
how_to_fix: Disable plain IMAP and enforce IMAPS (port 993) with TLS encryption
Require STARTTLS for all IMAP connections if port 143 must remain open
Implement account lockout policies after repeated failed authentication attempts
Regularly audit mail server logs for unusual access patterns
143.real_world_example: CVE-2021-38371 — Dovecot IMAP server vulnerability allowing crafted requests to crash or compromise the service

443.why_open: Encrypted web server traffic — standard port for secure web communication
443.who_uses: Web browsers and API clients for all secure web communication
443.who_exploits: Attackers targeting outdated TLS versions, weak cipher suites, or misconfigured certificates
443.risk: Misconfigured TLS can expose traffic to decryption; expired certificates cause service disruption and user warnings
how_to_fix: Disable TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 — enforce TLS 1.2 minimum, prefer TLS 1.3
Disable weak cipher suites — use only AEAD ciphers (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305)
Enable HSTS with a minimum max-age of 31536000 seconds
Monitor certificate expiry and automate renewal with certbot or equivalent
Run regular TLS configuration audits using testssl.sh or SSL Labs
443.real_world_example: CVE-2014-0160 — OpenSSL Heartbleed vulnerability exposing server memory contents including private keys

445.why_open: Windows file sharing and network communication protocol
445.who_uses: Windows networks for file sharing, printer sharing, and inter-process communication
445.who_exploits: Ransomware (WannaCry, NotPetya), worms, and attackers exploiting EternalBlue and related vulnerabilities
445.risk: Wormable exploitation enabling lateral movement, ransomware deployment, and complete network compromise
how_to_fix: Block port 445 at the network perimeter — never expose SMB to the internet
Disable SMBv1 immediately: Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB1Protocol $false
Apply MS17-010 patch if not already applied — eliminates EternalBlue attack vector
Require SMB signing to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks on internal networks
Segment the network to limit SMB exposure between untrusted hosts
445.real_world_example: CVE-2017-0144 — EternalBlue SMBv1 vulnerability exploited by WannaCry ransomware affecting 200,000+ systems globally

631.why_open: CUPS print server running and accepting print job submissions over the network
631.who_uses: Local network devices and users submitting print jobs to shared printers
631.who_exploits: Attackers sending malicious print jobs or exploiting CUPS vulnerabilities to achieve code execution
631.risk: Information disclosure, unauthorized print job submission, and potential remote code execution via CUPS exploits
how_to_fix: Disable CUPS if no printing functionality is required on this machine
Restrict CUPS to localhost only: set Listen localhost:631 in /etc/cups/cupsd.conf
Block port 631 on the external network interface via firewall rules
Keep CUPS updated to the latest version to patch known vulnerabilities
631.real_world_example: CVE-2023-32360 — CUPS unauthorized access vulnerability allowing retrieval of sensitive information

3306.why_open: MySQL database server accepting connections — potentially exposed to the network
3306.who_uses: Web applications, backend services, and database administrators
3306.who_exploits: Attackers attempting credential brute-force and direct database access from the internet
3306.risk: Direct database access from the network — complete data exfiltration, modification, or destruction
how_to_fix: Bind MySQL to localhost only: set bind-address = 127.0.0.1 in my.cnf
Never expose port 3306 to the public internet under any circumstances
Use strong, unique passwords for all database accounts
Remove anonymous accounts and the test database immediately
Access the database remotely via SSH tunnel rather than direct port exposure
3306.real_world_example: CVE-2012-2122 — MySQL authentication bypass allowing login with any password under certain conditions

3389.why_open: Windows Remote Desktop service accepting connections for graphical remote access
3389.who_uses: System administrators and remote workers accessing Windows desktops remotely
3389.who_exploits: Ransomware operators, nation-state actors, and automated scanners targeting exposed RDP for initial access
3389.risk: One of the most exploited entry points for ransomware — full graphical desktop access upon successful authentication
how_to_fix: Never expose RDP directly to the internet — place behind a VPN
Enable Network Level Authentication (NLA) to require credentials before session establishment
Change the default RDP port from 3389 to a non-standard port
Implement account lockout policies to prevent brute-force attacks
Enable RDP logging and monitor for failed authentication attempts
3389.real_world_example: CVE-2019-0708 — BlueKeep, a wormable RDP vulnerability enabling unauthenticated remote code execution on Windows 7 and Server 2008

5432.why_open: PostgreSQL database server accepting network connections
5432.who_uses: Web applications, data pipelines, and backend services requiring relational data storage
5432.who_exploits: Attackers targeting exposed database ports for credential attacks and direct data access
5432.risk: Full database compromise — all stored data accessible, modifiable, or deletable by an unauthorized party
how_to_fix: Restrict PostgreSQL to localhost: set listen_addresses = 'localhost' in postgresql.conf
Configure pg_hba.conf to reject all connections from non-local addresses
Use strong passwords for all PostgreSQL roles — enforce password policies
Never expose PostgreSQL directly to the internet — use SSH tunneling for remote access
Enable SSL for all PostgreSQL connections even on internal networks
5432.real_world_example: CVE-2019-9193 — PostgreSQL COPY TO/FROM PROGRAM feature enabling arbitrary OS command execution

5900.why_open: Remote desktop sharing protocol providing graphical control over a remote system
5900.who_uses: IT support teams and administrators for remote desktop assistance and management
5900.who_exploits: Attackers exploiting weak or absent authentication to gain full graphical control of the target machine
5900.risk: Complete remote control of the desktop — often configured with weak or no authentication at all
how_to_fix: Never expose VNC directly to the internet — tunnel through SSH or a VPN
Enforce strong, unique passwords for all VNC sessions
Use VNC implementations that support TLS encryption (e.g., TigerVNC with TLS)
Restrict VNC access to specific trusted IP addresses via firewall rules
Disable VNC entirely when remote desktop access is not actively required
5900.real_world_example: CVE-2019-15681 — RealVNC vulnerability allowing heap corruption and potential remote code execution

8080.service: HTTP Alternate — Development or Proxy Web Server
8080.why_open: Secondary web server or reverse proxy commonly used for development environments or application servers
8080.who_uses: Developers running local servers, Tomcat application servers, and HTTP proxy configurations
8080.who_exploits: Attackers targeting development servers with weaker security configurations than production environments
8080.risk: Development servers often lack authentication, expose debug endpoints, and run with elevated privileges
how_to_fix: Do not expose development servers to the public internet
Require authentication on all web interfaces running on port 8080
Disable debug endpoints and verbose error messages in any internet-facing deployment
Use a reverse proxy (Nginx, Apache) in front of application servers
Apply the same security standards to development servers as production
8080.real_world_example: CVE-2020-1938 — Apache Tomcat AJP connector vulnerability (Ghostcat) enabling file read and remote code execution

8443.service: HTTPS Alternate — Secure Development or Admin Interface
8443.why_open: Alternate HTTPS port commonly used for administrative web interfaces and development servers with TLS
8443.who_uses: Application servers, admin dashboards, and development environments requiring encrypted access
8443.who_exploits: Attackers scanning for exposed admin panels and management interfaces with default or weak credentials
8443.risk: Exposed admin interfaces can lead to full application or server compromise if default credentials remain unchanged
how_to_fix: Change all default credentials on admin interfaces immediately
Restrict access to port 8443 via firewall rules to trusted IP addresses only
Implement multi-factor authentication on administrative interfaces
Keep the underlying application server and TLS libraries updated
Use a Web Application Firewall (WAF) in front of admin interfaces where possible
8443.real_world_example: CVE-2021-44228 — Log4Shell, frequently exploited via web admin interfaces running on alternate HTTPS ports

161.why_open: Used for monitoring and managing network devices such as routers, switches, and servers
161.who_uses: Network administrators and monitoring systems (e.g., Nagios, Zabbix) to collect device metrics
161.who_exploits: Attackers exploiting default community strings or misconfigured SNMP services to gather sensitive information or perform attacks
161.risk: Exposure of network topology, device configurations, and potential for unauthorized control of devices
how_to_fix: Change default community strings (e.g., 'public' and 'private') to strong, unique values
Restrict SNMP access to trusted IP addresses only via firewall rules
Use SNMPv3 which provides authentication and encryption instead of SNMPv1/v2c
Disable SNMP entirely if not required for network management
Regularly audit SNMP configurations and logs for unauthorized access attempts
161.real_world_example: CVE-2017-7921 — SNMP service vulnerability allowing remote attackers to gain sensitive information from affected devices

2121.service: Alternative FTP / FTP Proxy / Custom File Transfer Service
2121.why_open: Commonly used as an alternative FTP control port to avoid conflicts with the default FTP port (21) or to run multiple FTP services
2121.who_uses: System administrators, FTP servers (e.g., ProFTPD, vsftpd), embedded devices, NAS systems, and application-specific file transfer services
2121.who_exploits: Attackers scanning for exposed FTP services, weak credentials, anonymous login, directory traversal, or vulnerable FTP server software
2121.risk: Unauthorized file access, credential theft, malware upload, data exfiltration, and potential remote code execution if the FTP service is vulnerable
how_to_fix: Disable anonymous FTP access unless absolutely required
Use strong authentication and unique passwords
Prefer SFTP or FTPS instead of plain FTP for encrypted communication
Restrict access to trusted IP addresses using firewall rules
Keep FTP server software updated with the latest security patches
Disable the service if it is no longer required
Monitor FTP logs for suspicious login attempts and file operations
2121.real_world_example: Many internet-exposed FTP servers running on alternative ports such as 2121 have been compromised through weak credentials and anonymous access, allowing attackers to steal or upload malicious files.

2222.why_open: Used as an alternative SSH port for secure remote administration, automation, file transfers, or to reduce automated scanning on the default SSH port (22)
2222.who_uses: System administrators, DevOps engineers, cloud servers, Linux administrators, developers, and automation tools using SSH or SFTP
2222.who_exploits: Attackers performing brute-force attacks, exploiting weak passwords, stolen SSH keys, or vulnerabilities in outdated SSH implementations
2222.risk: Unauthorized remote access, privilege escalation, data theft, lateral movement within the network, and complete server compromise if credentials are obtained
how_to_fix: Disable password authentication and use SSH key-based authentication
Disable direct root login (PermitRootLogin no)
Restrict SSH access to trusted IP addresses using firewall rules
Enable multi-factor authentication (MFA) where possible
Use fail2ban or similar tools to block repeated login attempts
Keep the SSH server updated with the latest security patches
Monitor SSH logs regularly for unauthorized access attempts
2222.real_world_example: Numerous ransomware groups and botnets continuously scan alternative SSH ports such as 2222 to identify exposed servers and perform brute-force attacks against weak credentials.
